profile.summary: PRIME is an evaluation framework for protein language models on a single viral protein: the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor binding domain. Frozen embeddings from five protein language models, with and without domain-specific fine-tuning on 347,432 outbreak RBD sequences, feed a small multi-task network that predicts two deep mutational scanning phenotypes, ACE2 binding affinity and protein expression. The point of the framework is the split: because viral sequences are near-identical, a random split lets mutations at the same residue appear in training and test, so PRIME holds out whole residue positions instead and shows that the random-split numbers are inflated. It is useful to anyone reading reported fitness-prediction accuracy on viral proteins.

summary_quotes.text: This homology leads to “data leakage” in standard random validation splits, yielding inflated performance metrics that fail to translate into real-world biosurveillance utility.

Unlike random splits, where mutations at the same site can appear in both training and test sets, position-stratified splitting ensures that all mutations at a specific residue position are held out together.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, how well a protein language model's representation of an RBD sequence predicts a measured phenotype: ACE2 binding affinity and expression level from yeast display deep mutational scanning. Second, and the reason the framework exists, how much of that apparent accuracy comes from homology leakage. The same embeddings and the same regression head are evaluated under two split rules, a random split and a position-stratified split that holds out all mutations at a residue position together, and the gap between them is the measurement. The framework also tracks whether domain-specific fine-tuning on outbreak sequences recovers predictive signal, and whether the embeddings separate known viral lineages.

Our results demonstrate that performance metrics from random splits are highly inflated due to data leakage.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Three datasets. The outbreak dataset is 347,432 unique SARS-CoV-2 RBD sequences (spike residues 319 to 541) curated from GISAID and the Sequence Read Archive as of 3 February 2023, with duplicates and ambiguous sequences removed; it is used for fine-tuning and for lineage analysis, and is dominated by Omicron (52.70 per cent) and Delta (35.71 per cent). The DMS dataset supplies the labels: 116,257 unique RBD sequences with measured ACE2 binding affinity and 105,525 with quantified expression, from a published yeast display experiment. The betaCov dataset is 75 RBD sequences from diverse Sarbecovirus members, used for cross-species analysis rather than for the regression benchmark.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Frozen embeddings, taken from the last hidden layer or mean-pooled over residues, are fed to a fully connected network of five layers whose hidden size follows the embedding size, with ReLU activations, no dropout and mean squared error loss, predicting binding and expression jointly. Evaluation is 5-fold cross-validation over residue positions: positions are randomly partitioned into five subsets and a sequence joins the training or test side according to whether its mutated positions fall exclusively in that subset. Within each fold the network is reinitialised, trained for 1000 epochs at a learning rate of 1e-5, and scored on the fold's test set; the coefficient of determination and RMSE are computed per fold and averaged. The stratified evaluation was repeated under three fold-assignment seeds (0, 1 and 2) to check that results do not depend on the fold construction.

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: The random split flatters every model. For ESM-C 600M with mean embeddings, a random split gives a coefficient of determination of 0.7711 for binding affinity, while the same base model under the position-stratified split has no predictive signal at all and a negative value of -0.1050. Fine-tuning on the outbreak dataset restores part of it: for the same model the stratified binding figure rises to 0.1823 plus or minus 0.2149 with mean embeddings and 0.2087 plus or minus 0.1451 with sequence-level CLS embeddings. Table 1 reports both splits, both phenotypes, both embedding methods and the fine-tuned and non-fine-tuned conditions for all five models; many of the stratified values are negative. Separately, fine-tuning raised masked language modelling accuracy on RBD sequences from 5.06 per cent to 96.33 per cent for ESM-2 8M, while a BERT model trained from scratch on RBD sequences alone reached 94.09 per cent but failed on rare residues.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository installs as a Python package into a conda environment, with two requirement sets because the authors moved to newer GPUs during revision. Masked language modelling is run by calling the relevant lightning script, and the transfer-learning models take flags for the target phenotype, the learning rate, the number of epochs and the path to a pretrained masked language model checkpoint; the readme ships SLURM examples because the work was done in a SLURM environment. The split comparison lives in its own directory: reading split_comparison.py, it wraps the multi-task fully connected head from the package, sets torch and numpy seeds, trains with Adam under a summed binding and expression mean squared error loss, and uses scikit-learn's KFold and train_test_split to build the two partitions. Its docstring warns that this random split is not the one used originally, so its values do not match the published random-split numbers.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two regimes over the same DMS data, both as 5-fold cross-validation rather than a fixed test set. The position-stratified split partitions residue positions into five subsets and assigns a sequence to training or test according to whether its mutated positions fall exclusively in that subset, so all mutations at a position are held out together. The random split is the comparison condition, in which mutations at the same site can appear on both sides. No per-fold test size is reported. Fold assignment was repeated under three seeds.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The position-stratified split is the control, and it is the point of the paper: all mutations at a given residue position are held out together, so a model cannot see another mutation at the same site during training. The paper is explicit that this measures generalisation to unseen positions rather than to unseen mutants. No sequence identity cut-off, clustering step or time split is applied, and the pretrained models' own training corpora are not screened against the DMS sequences. The 347,432-sequence outbreak set used for fine-tuning is drawn from the same protein as the test data by design.

quotes.text: Unlike random splits, where mutations at the same site can appear in both training and test sets, position-stratified splitting ensures that all mutations at a specific residue position are held out together.
where all mutations at specific residue positions are held out from the training set to measure genuine biological generalization.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Values are means across the five cross-validation folds with a standard deviation, which Table 1 prints for every cell. The spreads are large next to the differences being discussed: the fine-tuned ESM-C 600M stratified binding figure is 0.1823 plus or minus 0.2149. Fold-construction sensitivity was checked by repeating the stratified evaluation under three independent seeds, and the paper reports that the mutation count distributions stay consistent across seeds and folds. No bootstrap interval or statistical test between models is reported.

facts.value: The amino acid sequence of the RBD alone. The model sees it as a frozen embedding, either the last hidden layer or a mean over residues, and nothing else: no structure, no alignment and no metadata enters the regression head.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Two settings per model, reported side by side. Without fine-tuning, the released checkpoint's embeddings are frozen and only the regression head is trained, which makes it a linear-probe-style evaluation. With fine-tuning, the model is first adapted to RBD sequences by masked language modelling on the outbreak dataset (15 per cent of residues masked, AdamW, learning rate 1e-5, 100 epochs for ESM-RBD 8M and 15 epochs for the scaling tests, effective batch size 512 across eight A100 GPUs), and its embeddings are then frozen for the same head. BERT-RBD is trained from scratch as a control.

notes: One paper's framework, not a released suite: no leaderboard, so results_url is null. The sizes in the structured entries are the whole labelled dataset counts (116,257 binding and 105,525 expression sequences) because evaluation is 5-fold cross-validation and no per-fold test size is published; they must not be read as test-set sizes, and the two phenotypes have different counts. data_url is null: the outbreak sequences are behind a GISAID data set identifier and the DMS data come from a cited external study, with no open download address printed. The code licence is a Los Alamos government-contract notice followed by a grant in the exact wording of the MIT licence, and GitHub does not recognise it as a standard licence, so it is recorded as custom-permissive rather than MIT. One point for a reviewer: the published split_comparison.py says in its docstring that its random split differs from the paper's original random split and that the values do not match, so the repository cannot reproduce the published random-split column. The fine-tuned ESM-RBD models the paper reports as recovering signal are the authors' own contribution.
